videos.title: Stanford CS224N NLP with Deep Learning | Winter 2021 | Lecture 9 - Self- Attention and Transformers
videos.creator: Stanford Online
videos.why: University teaching on attention and Transformer architecture makes the tensor operations easier to explain in an interview.
videos.watchTask: Draw queries, keys, values and the attention output. Mark which positions an encoder or causal decoder can attend to; explain the purpose of a mask.
videos.practiceTask: Using a small Python list of attention scores, apply a causal mask before softmax. Show why a future token must receive zero probability.
videos.caution: This is a 2021 foundation lecture. It does not establish current model rankings or cover every later architecture.

evidence.note: Stanford Online video metadata identifies the lecture and its attention/Transformer topic.

videos.title: Diffusion and Score-Based Generative Models
videos.creator: MITCBMM; MIT OpenCourseWare resource; Yang Song
videos.why: A researcher explains score-based generation, neural score estimation and sampling rather than presenting only an image-generation interface.
videos.watchTask: Sketch the forward noising process and reverse sampling. Explain what a score function estimates and why generation takes multiple steps.
videos.practiceTask: In Python, add Gaussian noise to a one-dimensional synthetic distribution at several noise levels. Describe what a denoising model would have to learn; no model download is needed.
videos.caution: Theory prerequisites include probability and calculus. The lecture is not a turnkey Stable Diffusion application tutorial.

evidence.note: MIT names Yang Song, describes score estimation and SDE/MCMC sampling, and links this exact video.

videos.title: Stanford CS336 Language Modeling from Scratch | Spring 2025 | Lecture 4: Mixture of experts
videos.creator: Stanford Online; Tatsunori Hashimoto
videos.why: A dedicated university MoE lecture supports a precise explanation of routing and sparse computation.
videos.watchTask: Separate stored parameters from parameters active for one token. Trace the router decision and explain why uneven expert traffic can matter.
videos.practiceTask: Create a Python fixture of 12 tokens routed to four experts. Count loads and compare balanced versus concentrated routing; write the capacity assumptions.
videos.caution: Sparse activation does not automatically imply lower end-to-end latency. Compare actual hardware, routing and communication costs.

evidence.note: Stanford Online identifies Lecture 4 as Mixture of experts.
The archived university schedule lists Mixture of experts taught by Tatsu and links its slides.

videos.title: The State Space Model Revolution, with Albert Gu
videos.creator: The Cognitive Revolution; Albert Gu and Nathan Labenz
videos.why: A Mamba coauthor discusses selective state-space models, state size, training, inference and Mamba-2.
videos.watchTask: Write a state-update diagram. Explain what information is compressed into state and how this differs from retaining an attention KV cache.
videos.practiceTask: Implement a scalar recurrence s[t] = a*s[t-1] + b*x[t] in Python. Vary a and show how old inputs decay; identify why this is only a toy SSM, not a Mamba implementation.
videos.caution: This 2024 author discussion covers Mamba and Mamba-2. It is not a coding course, does not cover all later variants and does not prove universal superiority over attention.

evidence.note: Publisher page names Albert Gu and lists Mamba, state size, inference and Mamba-2 chapters.
Publisher-linked exact watch URL and episode identity.

videos.title: Lecture 7 | Training Neural Networks II
videos.creator: Stanford University School of Engineering; CS231n
videos.why: The lecture connects optimization behavior with momentum and adaptive optimizers; its official slides explicitly discuss saddle points.
videos.watchTask: Compare a local minimum with a saddle using gradient and curvature. Explain how momentum changes the update without promising that it always escapes every saddle.
videos.practiceTask: For f(x,y)=x*x-y*y, calculate the gradient and Hessian. Run a few Python gradient-descent and momentum steps from near zero and describe the trajectories.
videos.caution: The lecture predates many recent optimizers. Use it for mechanism and diagnostic reasoning; optimizer choice still requires task-specific experiments.

evidence.note: Official university video identifies the neural-network training lecture.
Official lecture slides show saddle points and subsequent momentum/optimizer material.

videos.title: AI Forum 2023 | Future of Foundation Models
videos.creator: Microsoft Research; Furu Wei
videos.why: A first-party research overview explicitly includes BitNet in the research agenda. It supplies historical context while the offline lesson provides the detailed mechanism.
videos.watchTask: Identify the BitNet portion and write which claim belongs to the original 2023 work. Keep it separate from later b1.58 and deployment results.
videos.practiceTask: Use Python to map illustrative weights to {-1,0,1}. Discuss scales, activation precision and accumulator precision; explain why ternary weights alone do not establish whole-system speed.
videos.caution: Supplemental historical overview, not a focused BitNet b1.58 coding tutorial. Do not infer b1.58 coverage, current model quality or CPU speedups from this talk. A focused first-party implementation-video gap remains.

evidence.note: Microsoft explicitly lists BitNet among the research shown and embeds this exact YouTube ID.
Microsoft identifies Furu Wei as the Future of Foundation Models speaker.
YouTube public oEmbed metadata confirms exact title and Microsoft Research channel.

videos.title: Building Production-Grade LLM Apps
videos.creator: DeepLearningAI; Pinecone and TruEra speakers
videos.why: A production-oriented workshop connects application quality, evaluation, monitoring and recovery using retrieval tooling examples.
videos.watchTask: Draw the retrieval-to-answer path. List a retrieval failure, an answer failure and a recovery action; identify which evidence each needs.
videos.practiceTask: Create ten local questions with expected source IDs and answerable/unanswerable labels. Score retrieval recall separately from answer support using fixed sample outputs.
videos.caution: Examples use Canopy and TruLens from the workshop era. SDKs and products can change; the offline exercise does not require those services or a live model.

evidence.note: Publisher event page names Pinecone/TruEra, Canopy/TruLens, evaluation and monitoring topics.
First-party video and public oEmbed metadata confirm title and DeepLearningAI channel.

videos.title: Mitigating LLM Hallucinations with a Metrics-First Evaluation Framework
videos.creator: DeepLearningAI; Galileo speakers
videos.why: This workshop focuses on measuring hallucination and context quality rather than relying only on a prompt that asks for accuracy.
videos.watchTask: Separate unsupported claims, missing required facts and irrelevant context. Explain why a model-based judge needs calibration against human-reviewed examples.
videos.practiceTask: Label six fixed answers against supplied evidence. Build a Python score table with unsupported-claim count and completeness, then inspect disagreements between rubric scores.
videos.caution: Vendor demonstrations are examples, not independent guarantees. Groundedness and factual correctness are different, and a judge can make mistakes.

evidence.note: DeepLearningAI metadata names the metrics framework and describes data/context quality, hallucination evaluation and guardrail demonstrations.

videos.title: LLMOps (LLM Bootcamp)
videos.creator: The Full Stack; Josh Tobin
videos.why: The publisher explicitly teaches choosing a base LLM across quality, speed, cost, tunability and security.
videos.watchTask: Turn those five dimensions into decision criteria for one application. Explain why the highest general benchmark score may not win your workload.
videos.practiceTask: Score three fictional model candidates on a fixed local task set. Apply hard privacy and latency constraints before comparing weighted quality and illustrative costs.
videos.caution: The course is from 2023. Historical prices, named models and API examples are not current procurement evidence; retain the decision method.

evidence.note: Publisher identifies Josh Tobin, includes the base-LLM selection chapter and links this exact video.

videos.title: HNSW for Vector Search Explained and Implemented with Faiss (Python)
videos.creator: James Briggs; published with Pinecone learning material
videos.why: A focused Python/Faiss tutorial explains HNSW graph search and its tuning tradeoffs.
videos.watchTask: Draw a small layered graph and trace a search. Separate construction settings from search-time effort, then connect each to recall, memory and latency.
videos.practiceTask: On a tiny local vector fixture, compute exact top-k neighbors. Compare simulated candidate subsets against the exact baseline and calculate recall@k before discussing speed.
videos.caution: This explains HNSW/Faiss; it is not evidence that Pinecone currently uses this index internally. Benchmark results depend on data and settings.

evidence.note: Primary learning article embeds the exact video and documents HNSW implementation with Faiss.
Exact watch page identifies the HNSW explanation and Python implementation.

videos.title: Composite Indexes and the Faiss Index Factory
videos.creator: James Briggs; Pinecone learning series
videos.why: A focused Faiss tutorial shows how indexing components can be composed, including inverted-file and quantization approaches.
videos.watchTask: Explain what a coarse partition does and why searching only some partitions can miss true neighbors. Separate IVF partitioning from PQ compression.
videos.practiceTask: Make a Python fixture of points assigned to coarse centroids. Compare one-list versus several-list probing and record missed exact neighbors; no downloaded embeddings are required.
videos.caution: The tutorial is historical. Factory syntax and supported combinations should be checked against the installed Faiss version before implementation.

evidence.note: Primary article embeds this exact ID and teaches index-factory composites including IVF/PQ.
Public YouTube oEmbed confirms title and James Briggs creator.

videos.title: Best Indexes for Similarity Search in Faiss
videos.creator: James Briggs; Pinecone learning series
videos.why: A companion tutorial frames index choice as a measured recall, latency and memory tradeoff.
videos.watchTask: Write a benchmark table with an exact baseline, candidate indexes, dataset size and query workload. Identify what makes a comparison unfair.
videos.practiceTask: Given fictional measurements, reject any index below the required recall floor, then compare remaining latency and memory. Label all supplied measurements illustrative.
videos.caution: Best means best for a measured workload, not a universal winner. The historical examples do not establish current vendor performance.

evidence.note: Primary article embeds this companion video while discussing composite-index tradeoffs.
Public YouTube oEmbed confirms exact title and James Briggs creator.

videos.title: RAG++ course: Hybrid search with Weaviate
videos.creator: CoreWeave channel; Weights & Biases RAG++ course
videos.why: A dedicated course segment introduces hybrid retrieval using Weaviate rather than treating embeddings as the only retrieval signal.
videos.watchTask: Find a query where an exact identifier favors lexical search and one where paraphrase favors vector search. Describe how combining rankings can help.
videos.practiceTask: Fuse two fixed local rankings using reciprocal rank fusion: sum 1/(c+rank), with c explicitly chosen. Compare results against lexical-only and dense-only lists.
videos.caution: The video uses provider integrations. The exercise uses offline rankings; SDK names and configuration may differ from the recording.

evidence.note: Creator video identifies the Weights & Biases RAG++ hybrid-search course segment; current public oEmbed attribution is CoreWeave.
Vendor documentation describes keyword, vector and hybrid search capabilities.

videos.title: Semantic search and reranking with Cohere and Pinecone
videos.creator: Pinecone
videos.why: A focused vendor-engineer demonstration shows semantic retrieval followed by reranking on financial documents.
videos.watchTask: Separate first-stage candidate recall from second-stage relevance ordering. Explain why a reranker cannot recover a relevant document absent from its candidates.
videos.practiceTask: Use a fixed shortlist of five local documents with relevance labels. Compare initial and reranked order using reciprocal rank; inspect an excluded relevant document.
videos.caution: The recording uses Cohere Rerank 3.5 and hosted services. Reranking does not enforce ACLs, exact numerical constraints or financial authorization.

evidence.note: Pinecone video metadata names semantic search/reranking and describes the financial-data example.
Publisher notebook accompanies the reranking example.

videos.title: LangChain Data Loaders, Tokenizers, Chunking, and Datasets - Data Prep 101
videos.creator: James Briggs
videos.why: A coding tutorial focuses on document preparation, token-aware chunk lengths, overlap and recursive splitting.
videos.watchTask: Explain why character count and token count differ. Show how overlap can preserve boundary context while increasing storage and repeated prompt content.
videos.practiceTask: Split a local policy document at headings, then compare with fixed-size chunks. Count characters and use supplied token counts to calculate overlap overhead and context budget.
videos.caution: LangChain APIs in this 2023 recording may be outdated. The offline task uses strings and provided counts; it does not claim an exact tokenizer from character heuristics.

evidence.note: Creator metadata identifies data loaders, tokenizers, chunking and datasets, with token-length and recursive-chunking chapters.

videos.title: Going Meta Ep1: Cypher and SPARQL side by side
videos.creator: Neo4j; Jesús Barrasa
videos.why: A hands-on comparison loads a dataset into a property graph and an RDF store, then compares Cypher and SPARQL queries.
videos.watchTask: Represent one person-company relationship as both a property graph and RDF triples. Explain labels/properties versus predicates and identifiers.
videos.practiceTask: Write a Cypher pattern and a SPARQL triple pattern returning the same small local fixture. State the assumptions needed for their results to agree.
videos.caution: Property graphs and RDF are distinct data models. Similar query results do not mean identical semantics or automatic OWL reasoning.

evidence.note: Neo4j identifies Episode 1 and the side-by-side RDF/property-graph query exercise.
Presenter repository supplies episode code and materials.

videos.title: Going meta - Ep4: Ontology based reasoning 101
videos.creator: Neo4j; Jesús Barrasa
videos.why: A focused episode demonstrates basic ontology-based inference using Cypher.
videos.watchTask: Separate asserted facts from inferred facts. Trace one subclass-derived conclusion and state the inference rule used.
videos.practiceTask: On a local Python fixture, compute a small subclass transitive closure and infer an entity type. Record provenance for each derived fact and reject a deliberately cyclic assumption if your chosen rules require it.
videos.caution: Basic Cypher inferencing is not a complete OWL 2 reasoner. This selection does not certify full RDF/OWL/SPARQL standards coverage.

evidence.note: Primary publisher identifies Episode 4 and describes basic ontology inferencing with Cypher.
Neo4j channel identifies the ontology-reasoning episode.

videos.title: OpenAI DevDay 2024 | Structured outputs for reliable applications
videos.creator: OpenAI
videos.why: A first-party developer session explains producing outputs constrained by a JSON schema.
videos.watchTask: Separate syntactic validity, schema conformity, semantic correctness and authorization. Describe the application handling for refusal or incomplete output.
videos.practiceTask: Validate three fixed JSON examples locally: malformed JSON, schema-valid but semantically wrong data, and an authorized valid request. Add deterministic business checks after schema validation.
videos.caution: A valid schema does not establish truth or permission. APIs and supported schema features can change after the 2024 recording; no API call is required for the exercise.

evidence.note: Official OpenAI session metadata identifies structured outputs for reliable applications.
Current first-party guide describes schema-constrained output and application handling.

videos.title: Stanford CS336 Language Modeling from Scratch | Spring 2025 | Lecture 10: Inference
videos.creator: Stanford Online; Percy Liang
videos.why: A dedicated inference lecture gives systems context for token budgets, memory and serving decisions.
videos.watchTask: Separate processing the input from generating output tokens. Explain why request length and concurrency both matter when planning inference capacity.
videos.practiceTask: Use illustrative values to compute KV bytes = 2 * layers * KV_heads * head_dim * tokens * bytes_per_element. Then calculate a batch budget and reserve an explicit safety margin.
videos.caution: The formula exercise is a teaching task, not a benchmark claim. Real runtimes add overhead, sharing and compression; hardware-specific examples do not establish your SLO.

evidence.note: Stanford Online identifies the dedicated inference lecture.
University schedule identifies Lecture 10 Inference as taught by Percy and links lecture_10.py.

videos.title: OWASP Agentic AI CTF - FinBot DEMO: Goal Manipulation
videos.creator: Helen Oakley; endorsed by OWASP GenAI Security Project
videos.why: An OWASP-endorsed simulated financial-agent attack makes the boundary between untrusted instructions and permitted financial actions concrete.
videos.watchTask: Identify attacker input, victim agent, sensitive action and failed trust boundary. Explain which controls must execute outside the language model.
videos.practiceTask: Build a local Python payment-tool fixture using Decimal, an allowlisted account, amount ceiling, approval requirement and idempotency key. Feed it a malicious proposed action and verify rejection without moving money.
